claims.text: Alcohol consumption is inversely associated with fatty liver in Japanese men.
Forty percent of male nondrinkers had fatty liver compared to 28 percent of male drinkers.
There is a significant inverse correlation between alcohol drinking frequency and the prevalence of fatty liver in Japanese men.
Sixteen percent of female nondrinkers had fatty liver compared to 10 percent of female drinkers.
Drinking less than 20 grams of alcohol on 1 to 3 days per week is associated with a lower prevalence of fatty liver in Japanese women.

evidence.description: Alcohol consumption was inversely associated with fatty liver in men with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.54 (95% CI, 0.46-0.63).
In men, 40% of nondrinkers and 28% of drinkers had fatty liver.
The prevalence of fatty liver in men was 38% for 1-3 days/week, 29% for 4-6 days/week, and 24% for daily drinking, showing a significant inverse correlation (P < 0.001).
In women, 16% of nondrinkers and 10% of drinkers had fatty liver.
In women, drinking less than 20 g on 1-3 days/week was associated with low prevalence of fatty liver with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.47 (95% CI, 0.23-0.96).

methodologies.name: Cross-sectional ultrasonographic health checkup study
methodologies.description: A cross-sectional study evaluating the association between self-reported drinking pattern and ultrasonographically diagnosed fatty liver.
datasets: Japanese health checkup dataset (4957 men, 2155 women)
conditions: Exclusion of individuals with reported liver diseases
